bio.en: Jacob Warwick is a professional negotiator who works behind the scenes with senior tech execs, pro athletes, and celebrities to navigate complex comp, M&A, and enterprise-sales negotiations, having helped clients secure over $1 billion in additional compensation.
bio.zh: Jacob Warwick 是一位职业谈判专家，在幕后为科技高管、职业运动员和名人处理复杂的薪酬、并购与企业销售谈判，已帮助客户额外争取到超 10 亿美元的补偿。

summary.en: Jacob gets tactical about comp negotiation: never do it over email (you can't control tone, and context like an annoyed CEO in an airport line can poison it), and lead with the value you'll create, not just demands. He covers who should speak first when comp comes up, the costly mistakes people unknowingly make, and how to ask for more without seeming greedy ('What's the chance there could be a little more?'). The episode is a rare, under-the-radar masterclass in the psychology and mechanics of getting paid what you're worth.
summary.zh: Jacob 就薪酬谈判给出具体战法：绝不用邮件谈（你无法控制语气，而像机场排队中正恼火的 CEO 这样的语境会毁掉谈判），并应先讲你将创造的价值，而非只提要求。他讲到了薪酬话题出现时该谁先开口、人们不知不觉犯下的昂贵错误，以及如何在不显得贪婪的前提下要求加薪（“有没有可能稍微多一点点？”）。这期节目是一场地地道道、鲜为人知的、关于“如何拿到与你价值匹配报酬”的心理与技巧的公开课。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What's the most common mistake that people make when they're negotiating their comp?
turns.zh: 人们在谈判薪酬时最常犯的错误是什么？

turns.speaker: Jacob Warwick
turns.en: Often, we'll hide behind the easiest communication channel possible. I might email you my demands. The problem with that is I can't control tone. If I push back and the CEO that reads it is in the airport security line and pissed off and they read it, they might be like, "That bastard wants more money."
turns.zh: 通常，我们会选择最简便的沟通方式。比如，我可能会通过邮件向你提出我的要求。但问题在于，我无法控制邮件的语气。如果我据理力争，而读到邮件的CEO当时正排队过安检，情绪烦躁，看到这些要求时，可能会想：“这混蛋居然还想要更多钱。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: A lot of people listening to this are just afraid to ask. "For more, I'm going to come across as greedy. It's all going to fall apart."
turns.zh: 很多听众只是害怕开口要求：“要更多钱的话，会显得我很贪心。整个谈判可能会因此泡汤。”

turns.speaker: Jacob Warwick
turns.en: But when you look at the money that the company's making in comparison, you're not being greedy. It doesn't have to be such an aggressive thing. It doesn't have to be confrontational. The simplest advice, "What's the chance there could be a little more?" That's not greedy at all.
turns.zh: 但对比公司赚的钱，你的要求根本不算贪心。没必要太咄咄逼人，没必要剑拔弩张。最简单的建议是：“有没有可能再加一点？”这根本不算贪心。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The core to your philosophy is make it very clear to the company, "Here's the pain I will solve for you, and here's why it's worth paying me this much more."
turns.zh: 你的核心理念是，要向公司清晰传达：“我能为你解决什么痛点，因此你值得多付我这么多钱。”

turns.speaker: Jacob Warwick
turns.en: These companies have significant leverage over it. They know what people make, they know what others make, they know what they'll accept. You have to understand what value you can create. And if you understand that value, you can have that conversation with confidence.
turns.zh: 这些公司对此有很大的话语权。他们清楚别人拿多少钱，也清楚你能接受多少。你必须清楚自己能创造什么价值。只要你清楚自己的价值，就能自信地展开谈判。

turns.zh: 真的非常感激。这次活动绝对值回票价。对我们来说，最有价值的部分就是能从你这里汲取所有智慧。我们将深入探讨谈判技巧，如何更好地争取薪酬待遇，这不仅对薪酬谈判有益，还能应用到生活中的其他方面。就我个人而言，我在这方面一直做得很糟糕。我不知道……或许有一次我成功争取到了更高的薪酬，但总的来说我对这类谈判始终心怀恐惧，而且做得很不好。相信大多数听众也都对此感到紧张和无从下手，而你却以此为业。你帮助人们进行谈判，但我觉得很多人甚至不知道还有这种服务存在，更不知道有人能专业协助谈判。因此你见证过无数谈判实例。（00:05:19）顺便说一句，你的客户大多是资深人士，但我们要讨论的许多技巧都适用于任何职级的人。我先抛出一个问题，方便大家理解背景：当人们不主动争取薪酬时，通常会错失多少潜在利益？

turns.speaker: Jacob Warwick
turns.en: Yeah. So, typically, what I've seen is, even without my help, just general pushbacks, not aggressive, a simple, "What's the chance there could be more here?" kind of pushback. That's about as easy as it can get. You get the offer, you say, "What's the chance there's a little bit more?" Almost always see a 20% improvement on that, and that is across the board from earlier stage positions. Let's say they gave you a $100,000 offer, 120 could be there just from a simple pushback, which is, when you're making that kind of money, that's life changing. I've noticed that when you make $1 million W2, same pushback, 20%, sometimes more, just on the, "What's the chance?" depending on how well you navigated that interview process. (00:06:18): Now, on average, when I'm calculating out, what I'm looking for with clients is about 40% movement on an increase. We have seen as much as 100, 200, 300, 400% increases from initial offers, most notably, breaking salary bands, which we all treat as gospel, which is something we'll probably talk about through the course of this podcast today. Those that challenge authority and challenge in a meaningful and collaborative way will win more than those that don't. What's interesting is I've found that product, product leaders, engineers, designers, some of the more... tend to be more introverted and thoughtful types negotiate more poorly than the obnoxious marketers and revenue leaders and the more extroverted types. And it's frustrating because if you look back at the last, say, 25 years or so, product has really defined the tech generation in so many ways. This isn't to discredit marketers or anything like that. It's just to show that there's a couple of sides of the business, and everyone tends to negotiate a little differently. (00:07:28): You're looking back at your career and say, " The great Lenny had a tough time pushing back." I think that's actually inspiring for a lot of the listeners to see that you're not alone in feeling this. It doesn't have to be such an aggressive thing. It doesn't have to be confrontational. The simplest advice that I can give you is, "What's the chance there could be a little more?" That's not greedy at all. That's just a simple ask, and even that, 20, 30%.
turns.zh: 是的。所以，我通常看到的是，即便没有我的帮助，人们也会进行一些温和的反击，不是那种咄咄逼人的，而是简单地问：“这里还有可能再加点吗？”这种反击方式最容易操作。收到 offer 后，你可以说：“这里还有可能再加一点吗？”这种方法几乎能让薪资涨幅增加 20%，而且这种效果在早期职位上普遍适用。比如说，如果他们给你 10 万美元的 offer，通过这种简单反击，涨幅可能达到 12 万美元——当你赚这么多钱时，这简直能改变人生。我注意到，当你的 W2 薪资达到 100 万美元时，同样的反击策略也能带来 20%的涨幅，有时甚至更多，这取决于你在面试过程中的表现。（00:06:18）现在，平均而言，我为客户计算的涨幅目标是 40%。但我们也见过初始 offer 涨幅高达 100%、200%、300%、400% 的案例，尤其是打破薪资范围的情况——我们都把这视为行业常识，这也是我们今天在播客中要探讨的话题。那些敢于挑战权威、以富有意义且合作的方式提出质疑的人，最终收获会比不这样做的人多得多。令人欣慰的是，我发现产品、产品经理、工程师、设计师等更内向、善于思考的人，在谈判中表现往往不尽如人意，而那些爱出风头、强势的市场营销人员和销售主管则更善于谈判。这很令人沮丧，因为回顾过去 25 年左右，产品在很多方面定义了科技行业的一代人。当然，这并不是要贬低市场营销人员之类的人，而是想说明商业世界有两面性，每个人在谈判中的方式确实有所不同。（00:07:28）当你回顾自己的职业生涯时会说：“伟大的莱尼在反击方面遇到了困难。” 我认为，这对很多听众来说很鼓舞人心，因为他们会发现自己并非孤例。这不必是一种激进的做法，也不必充满对抗。我能给出的最简单的建议就是：“这里还有可能再加一点吗？” 这根本不是贪婪。这只是一个简单的请求，即便如此，也能带来 20%、30% 的涨幅。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So, again, a lot of people listening to this are just afraid to ask for more. There's like, "I'm going to come across as greedy. It's all going to fall apart. They're going to be like, 'What are you talking about? No, no, forget it,'" or they join... They get better comp and then they're like, "Oh, everyone can... They know that I pushed all this and I'm this kind of greedy person, and now the expectations are higher." What do you tell people to help them get past that and actually negotiate and actually go for it?
turns.zh: 所以，再说一次，许多听众只是害怕要求更多。他们会想：“我会显得很贪婪。一切都会搞砸。他们会说，‘你说什么呢？不，不，别想了。’” 或者他们加入……获得了更好的薪酬后，又会说：“哦，每个人都能……他们知道我为此努力了，是个贪婪的人，现在期望值更高了。” 你会怎么告诉人们，帮助他们克服这种心理，真正去谈判、去争取？

turns.speaker: Jacob Warwick
turns.en: Yeah, a couple things here. So, first of all, usually a company is extracting much more value out of you naturally, like 5 to 1, 10 to 1, 100 to 1. I know the audience is primarily product here. You're developing products that have infinite scalability in some capacity that's going to make the company a lot of money, and you're a big piece of that. Product tends to be rewarded fairly well. But when you look at the money that the company's making in comparison, you're not being greedy. And if you understand that value exchange, you can have that conversation with confidence. That's not to say that being a tall poppy isn't risky. That's the term. You over negotiate. I would rather my clients over-negotiate, reach a couple rungs up on the ladder, and they get slapped down. They're still failing forward, and they're growing in some capacity. (00:09:14): If you can ideally align work that doesn't feel like work, it feels a little bit more like play with strong compensation, you don't always need to negotiate hellaciously for the top of the band or break the bands just because you can. This isn't to be greedy, but it's just to understand that this value exchange isn't fair for you regardless of how it works. The path to wealth is through ownership. And as a W2 employee, you're being taxed heavily, and it makes sense to push a little bit in this context. That's typically where I start. I want you to just have the confidence to know that it's okay.
turns.zh: 是啊，这里有几点需要说明。首先，通常公司会从你身上榨取更多价值，比例可能是5比1、10比1、100比1。我知道听众主要来自产品领域。你们开发的产品在某种程度上具有无限的扩展性，能为公司赚大钱，而你们在其中扮演着重要角色。产品部门的待遇通常很不错。但当你看看公司赚的钱和你相比时，觉得自己要求高并不过分。如果你能理解这种价值交换，就能自信地进行谈判。这并不是说出头会没有风险——就是所谓的“出头鸟”现象。你可能过度谈判了。我宁愿客户过度谈判，爬上几个台阶后被打压下来。他们仍在不断进步，取得一定成长。（00:09:14）理想情况下，如果你能找到不像工作的工作，能在高薪下享受些许乐趣，你没必要为了拿高薪或突破薪资上限而拼命谈判。这不是贪婪，而是要明白无论怎样的谈判结果，公司都占了上风。致富之路在于拥有自己的资产。作为W2员工，你要承担高额税负，在这种情况下适当争取是合理的。这通常是我的出发点。我希望你们能自信地知道，这样做没问题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let me come at it from the other direction. A lot of people listening to this podcast are founders or hiring managers, managers. They may not be super excited to hear or giving people advice on how to negotiate harder for higher comp. What could you say to them to make them feel a little bit better about us sharing this sort of advice?
turns.zh: 让我从另一个角度说。很多听这个播客的人是创始人或招聘经理、部门主管。他们可能不太乐意听到或听别人建议如何更强硬地争取高薪。对于我们分享这类建议，他们可能不太自在。你能对他们说些什么，让他们对我们分享这类建议感觉好一些呢？

turns.speaker: Jacob Warwick
turns.en: I will challenge them as well. Now, how important of a priority is top talent and maintaining and retaining top talent to you? When we're thinking about how quickly the speed of innovation is happening, you've had a lot of great AI guests on the channel recently, right? The exponential curve of growth is increasing. If you hope to stand a chance, you need to attract the top talent and you need to keep that top talent because it's very expensive to replace them. I'm not suggesting that people beat you up for the sake of beating you up. This is a myth about negotiation that's adversarial. What I teach is how can we be more collaborative, so the conversation is, "Look, Lenny, as a founder, can you help me understand what's important to you, the value that this work will drive, and then naturally we'll come to terms that make a little bit more of a value exchange makes sense there." (00:11:03): Oftentimes, some of the ways that we're breaking the boundaries of compensation isn't necessarily advocating for a busted base comp level and bonus percentage. Oftentimes, we're putting performance incentives, milestone triggers. If the company grows to 100 million ARR and I contributed this to it, what would that outcome look like? Would that be another tranche of stock or would that be cash or would that... We are getting more creative here. What's interesting is, for the longest time, I had a difficult time advocating for this. And having been a CEO and founder myself, I understand why you don't want to do it because it's hard. It's hard to make this. Everyone also thinks they're top talent. And when everyone thinks they're top talent, somebody's got to be lying. It can be difficult to understand that. So those that I've found are more confident to push towards performance-based tend to have more skin in the game, tend to want to stick around and see that success happen. Those are the types of people I want working for me if I want to be a very competitive organization. (00:12:09): I have started to have these conversations with a couple of Fortune 500 companies as well as some talent consulting companies, think big recruiting firms, where they've brought me in to advise on the comp committees so that they can get more creative with their structure so they don't lose talent. Because nobody wins when you hire a top performer and they leave in 10 months. The recruiting firm loses their pay, their performance pay. The company now has to go back and replace that person. It usually costs hundreds of thousands. And in some of the realms that we navigate in the Fortune 500, it will cost millions, if not tens of millions, to replace the lost IP there. So the argument here is, "It's okay to get creative. Reward it when you see it." I'm not suggesting give everyone everything in the company and totally ruin your business model. But if you want to be competitive, be competitive with your pay as well.
turns.zh:
我也会向他们提出挑战。那么，对你而言，顶尖人才以及留住和培养顶尖人才的优先级有多高？当我们思考创新速度的急剧变化时，你最近在节目中邀请了许多优秀的AI领域嘉宾，对吧？指数级增长的曲线正在不断攀升。如果你想在竞争中立足，就必须吸引并留住顶尖人才，因为替换他们成本极高。我不是说要以打击对手为目的，这只是一种对抗性谈判的误区。我所教授的是如何通过更具协作性的方式达成共识。比如：“听着，莱尼，作为创始人，你能否帮助我理解对你而言重要的是什么，这项工作的价值所在，然后自然而然地达成一个让价值交换更合理的协议。”  
（00:11:03）：很多时候，我们突破薪酬界限的方式并非一定要提高基本薪资和奖金比例。更多的是设置绩效激励机制和里程碑触发条件。比如，如果公司营收增长至1亿美元，而我为此做出了贡献，会有怎样的结果？是再发放一批股票？还是现金奖励？……我们在这方面正变得越来越有创意。令人感兴趣的是，很长一段时间以来，我都难以为此争取支持。作为CEO和创始人，我理解你为何不愿这么做，因为这确实不易。这种创新很难实现。每个人都自视为顶尖人才，而当所有人都这么认为时，必然有人在说谎。这点很难理解。因此，那些更自信推行绩效激励的人往往更全身心投入，愿意留下来见证成功。如果我想打造一个极具竞争力的组织，我希望这样的员工为我效力。  
（00:12:09）：我已经开始与多家《财富》500强企业以及一些人才咨询公司（比如大型招聘机构）展开对话。他们邀请我为薪酬委员会提供建议，以便在薪酬结构上更具创新性，避免人才流失。因为聘请了顶尖人才却在10个月后离职，对招聘公司和企业都是损失——前者失去了佣金，后者需要重新招聘替代人员。通常这类成本高达数十万美元。在《财富》500强企业的某些领域，替换失去的知识产权可能需要数百万甚至数千万美元。因此，我的观点是：“可以适当创新，看到价值时就给予奖励。” 我并非建议给公司所有人发钱彻底毁掉商业模式，但如果你想保持竞争力，就必须在薪酬方面也做到竞争力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's a great answer. We were chatting before we started recording this and you shared that you've helped people negotiate with many of the guests on this podcast, like people that they were hiring, and you helped them get higher comp.
turns.zh: 这回答得真棒。我们录制前聊过，你提到曾帮助许多播客嘉宾进行薪酬谈判，比如他们要招聘的人员，最终你帮助他们获得了更高的薪酬。

turns.speaker: Jacob Warwick
turns.en: I won't mention any names. Some recently were in the realm of 10 million-plus on increases in compensation across a team of just a handful of folks, again, Fortune 500, but the alternative was lose them to competitors and have the stock drop after the CEO made announcements publicly in their earnings calls. They don't know that they may have cost them 10 million today, but it saved them 300-plus, 300, 500, in this business process, so the success will be there. And I would say almost anybody would pay 10 to save 300.
turns.zh: 我就不点名了。最近有几家公司，其团队规模不大，但加薪幅度却高达千万级别——这都是《财富》500强企业。但如果不这样做，员工可能会跳槽到竞争对手那里，而且在CEO公开财报电话会议时宣布加薪后，股价还会暴跌。员工或许不知道自己今天损失了1000万美元，但通过这种商业策略，他们节省了300多万美元的成本，最终成果显著。几乎所有人都会愿意花1000万美元来节省300万美元。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And the way you operate, just so people understand, is you're very behind the scenes. You work with clients and you advise them. You're never involved in the negotiation, you just give them advice on how to approach it.
turns.zh: 再说说你的工作方式。大家可能不太清楚，你的工作极具隐蔽性。你与客户合作，为他们提供建议，但从不参与谈判过程，只是指导他们如何推进谈判。

turns.speaker: Jacob Warwick
turns.en: I would call it fingerprintless, and there's a reason for this. It's not yet popularized. Maybe it will be with some of these in AI ICEs, and these hot scientists are pulling down $100 million contracts. Maybe this will change soon. In Hollywood, you have an agent negotiate on your behalf, and they kind of are serving as that middle mediator. That's not common in the corporate America right now. Now, if that happens, it almost dilutes the leadership and presence of the executive. So how I work is similar to an attorney where all correspondence goes through me before it goes to the end recipient. Let's say that you're going to talk to the CEO, you call me first. We prepare the game plan, we strategize, you then perform, then we debrief. Then the CEO sends you an email. That email comes to me. We draft it together. (00:14:59): I usually test my client's instincts first rather than just doing the work for them, test their instincts, polish the language, because every step of the way is a negotiation. Now, this also slows the process down. We want to go slower, and I'm sure we'll talk a little bit more about that in the podcast too. Haste equals risk. As you slow down, oftentimes, we want to take a couple of days to respond not to be a jerk or belligerent or to manufacture some fake urgency, but it shows a little scarcity and thought process to your time, and we get to calculate and collect information through the process.
turns.zh: 我称之为“无痕谈判”，之所以这样叫，是因为这种方式尚未普及。或许在AI领域的初创公司中会流行起来，那些热门科学家能拿下1亿美元的合同。这种情况可能很快就会改变。好莱坞通常由经纪人代表客户谈判，充当中间人的角色。但目前美国企业界这种模式并不常见。若引入这种机制，可能会削弱高管的领导力和影响力。我的工作方式类似于律师事务所，所有信件都需先经我转交再送达最终收件人。比如，你要和CEO沟通，先给我打电话。我们一起制定谈判策略，执行后再进行总结。CEO发邮件时，邮件也会先发给我，我们共同润色措辞。（00:14:59）我通常先测试客户的谈判直觉，而不是直接代劳，帮助他们提升语言表达能力，因为谈判的每一步都是博弈过程。这也会拖慢进程，但我们希望放慢节奏。稍后我们会在播客中深入探讨这个话题。急功近利往往会带来风险。放慢节奏时，我们会留出几天时间回复信息，不是故意刁难或制造虚假紧迫感，而是展现出对时间的重视，通过这个过程收集信息、权衡利弊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is so interesting. What's the most common biggest mistake that people make when they're negotiating their comp?
turns.zh: 这个问题很有意思。在薪酬谈判中，人们最常犯的错误是什么？

turns.speaker: Jacob Warwick
turns.en: They don't understand when it starts. It starts much sooner than you think. I've got myself on hot water with this before too because a... A LinkedIn profile in your resume is a snapshot of what you've been in the past, but it doesn't help you negotiate in the forward. So if somebody can say, "Oh, I'm looking at Lenny, and I'm looking at product manager." If that's all they saw, they're not going to know all this work that you're doing in the future moving forward and what your visions are and things like that, so they stamp you as Product Manager Lenny. Now, you're media mogul icon, whatever, but there's a gap that you have to fill. The things you say on LinkedIn serve as a perception. The headshot that you have serves as a perception. I used to joke that I could scan profiles. I would know how much money someone made by the quality of their headshot. You can see... It was wildly consistent. It was almost frustrating. (00:16:40): But anyway, what you're putting out into the world, the narrative you share publicly, starts to become how you're known, your reputation. If you are positioned as a commodity, you will be treated like a commodity. Oftentimes, the less you share is better because when you're on the phone with somebody, you can correct the narrative and steer the conversation where you want it to go versus have to live by the sins of what you did 10 years ago, as an example. So the things you share with recruiters, they take notes. When a recruiter calls you and says, "Hey, Lenny, how much money do you expect to make?" and you say, "Oh, 225, that sounds fair." Five years later, they call you and they expect you to make 225 again, not recognizing that you've grown exponentially since then. So everything you communicate starts to serve as that value chain across the board. (00:17:32): Another mistake that people make, and you mentioned this a little earlier, it feels uncomfortable to get, quote, unquote, "confrontational" or to feel like you're asking for too much, so often we'll hide behind the easiest communication channel as possible. I might email you my demands or my negotiation, and the problem with that is I can't control tone. I can't control... especially when you're negotiating at high levels. If I push back and the CEO that reads it is in the airport security line and pissed off and they read it, they might be like, "That bastard wants more money." That's all they take away. Even if you perfectly worded it, you got it all as clean as it can be, if you catch them at the wrong time, you have no control over how it's received. So it's always better to have at least a video call, if not in person, so you can share tone, you can read body language, you can correct every step of the way. (00:18:32): Oftentimes, we also try to negotiate through recruiters. You could do that... I did the thing, Jacob. I talked to a recruiter. I spent a half an hour explaining it. The problem with that is you're playing a game of telephone, so the same thing happens. I explain it to the recruiter. I get the tone right. The recruiter goes to the CEO and says, "That bastard wants more money," and that's all they communicate. People negotiate with the wrong folks. You have to go to the one who has skin in the game. Who controls the P&L? Who controls EBITDA? What's their motivation? That's who you want to talk to. Some people might also have a concern with, "Well, how do I go around the recruiter? I don't want them to look bad." We have to do that respectfully and now we need to plan what that communication looks like. The important thing here is just because it's uncomfortable doesn't mean you don't need to do it. It just means you don't know how to do it. So when something's uncomfortable, you have to run towards that because that's where the growth happens.
turns.zh:
他们不明白谈判何时开始。谈判往往比你想象的更早开始。我自己也曾因此陷入过困境，因为……在简历中附上领英资料固然能展示你的过往经历，但却无法助你把握未来谈判的主动权。若对方只看到“我在领英上的职位是产品经理”，而忽视你未来可能的远见与发展，他们就会把你定型为“产品经理莱尼”。即便你后来转型为媒体大亨或其他角色，依然存在认知鸿沟。简历上的信息只是冰山一角，头像照更是定型标签。我曾开玩笑说能通过头像判断薪资水平——这种现象高度一致，甚至令人沮丧。  

（00:16:40）但你向外界传递的信息、公开分享的叙事将成为你的品牌标签。若被定位为可替代品，就注定被当作商品对待。越是隐藏真实需求，越容易被动接受。例如，招聘者打来电话问“莱尼，你期望薪资多少？”你说“22.5万”看似合理，五年后对方却按老数据套用，完全忽视你的指数级成长。信息传递必须形成全方位的价值链。  

（00:17:32）另一个常见误区——你提到过——人们总因“过于强势”而退缩。邮件谈判无法控制语气与肢体语言，尤其在高层谈判中。若对方在机场安检排队时看到你的要求，可能直接认为“这混蛋要加钱”。即便措辞完美，时机不对也会功亏一篑。因此，至少要通过视频通话沟通，直观传达语气与意图。  

（00:18:32）招聘代理常充当缓冲，但这其实是“传声筒”游戏。即便你详细解释，HR也可能只截取“混蛋要钱”这句话。谈判对象必须是掌握核心权力的人：谁管控损益表？谁掌控息税前利润？他们的动机才是关键。切忌与“中间人”纠缠，直击核心决策者才是正解。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love how tactical we're getting here. Following this thread, the advice here is when you get an offer and you want, and you should... Basically, you're saying you should always negotiate. In some way, you should push back. Your advice here is don't do it over email, make sure you find a way to do a video call with essentially the hiring manager or the person that has skin in the game, like the finances and the budget.
turns.zh: 我很欣赏我们在这里的谈判技巧。根据这条讨论线索，建议是当你收到录用通知后，如果你想争取更多权益，就应该...基本上就是说要始终保持谈判姿态。某种程度上，你需要反击。你的建议是别通过邮件沟通，一定要找到机会与招聘经理或对预算和财务有决策权的人进行视频通话。

turns.speaker: Jacob Warwick
turns.en: There are situations, especially at high levels, more deals are closed on the golf course than they are in a boardroom. There are situations where you pull someone into a different element. This is called home field advantage. So if you go to a company to have a conversation, you are out of your element in a situation where you may not perform your best. The other thing people don't do is they don't control the time of which they have a conversation, "CEO wants to hop on at 6:00 in the morning, get your ass up, get that presentation, and go." You need to say, "I'm not available at that time." And you read your own body language, " I'm strongest between the hours of 10:00 AM and 1:00 PM. I want a meeting in that time," so I will say, "I'm unavailable until that time becomes available." That also communicates scarcity and that you won't get pushed around. It's scary to do that, to say, "No," to the CEO, "I'm actually only available here," but that also creates a rubber band effect that makes you more attractive. (00:20:55): Actually, OpenAI did this, which is funny, and I didn't realize what the reason was, but I had some clients interviewing for C-suite roles at OpenAI, and so pushing Sam Altman around a little bit, which I'm okay with. I'm okay with that. So they used to walk outside of the office and just walk downtown San Francisco instead. You take someone out of the element, you get the endorphins going, you're walking and talking. The important piece here is instead of you and I being confrontational, like negotiating between each other, we're walking side by side. So it's almost like you could put your arm around the other person, you're solving the problem together. These sound like minor things to consider, but the body language and the tone and the collaboration and the energy starts to flow more naturally when you do. This is all behavioral psychology. (00:21:45): Funny story, why I found out OpenAI did that was because they didn't want any executives going into the office because it was such a mess. It was the biggest startup you've ever seen. I used to joke that it was two midgets in a trench coat pretending to be a real company. Anyway, the point was let's take them to a place where we can control and have an advantage over the conversation. So that's a way that you can think about, "Where are you going to feel most comfortable? What hours of the day are you most comfortable?" If you can bring someone to a lunch or a coffee where you're on even playing field or even your home field, you will perform better in those situations and you have more control over that than you may think.
turns.zh: 有些情况下，尤其是在高层级别，更多交易是在高尔夫球场上达成的，而非董事会会议室里。还有些时候，你会把对方带入不同的环境。这叫做主场优势。所以当你去公司谈判时，你其实处于不利位置，可能无法发挥最佳状态。人们常忽视的是，他们无法控制谈判的时间安排——“CEO想在早上6点开会，你得赶紧起来准备演示文稿然后去汇报。”你应该说：“我那个时候没空。”然后观察自己的肢体语言：“我上午10点到下午1点状态最佳，咱们约个时间吧。”这样既传达了时间紧迫感，又表明自己不愿被随意摆布。（00:20:55）：说到这儿，有个趣事儿。OpenAI就这么做过，我之前都没意识到原因何在。有客户去OpenAI面试高管职位，他们故意带萨姆·奥特曼到旧金山市中心散步，这招我倒不介意。这样做能让人脱离舒适区，释放内啡肽，边走边谈。关键在于不要对峙式谈判，而是并肩协作。比如你可以挽着对方，共同解决问题。这些看似微不足道的细节，实则能让肢体语言、语气、协作精神和能量更自然流畅。这都是行为心理学的奥秘。（00:21:45）：说起来，我发现OpenAI这么做的原因是他们不想让高管们待在混乱的办公室里。那可是你见过规模最大的初创公司。我常开玩笑说，那俩家伙就像披着风衣的侏儒， pretend to be a real company anyway. 总之，关键在于把谈判环境控制在自己有优势的场合。比如你最自在的时段、最习惯的场合。若能把对方带到午餐或咖啡馆，让双方处于平等甚至主场环境，你就能在这种情境下发挥得更好，掌控局面也比想象中更容易。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So the advice there is try to get this conversation out of their office.
turns.zh: 所以建议是尽量把谈判移出对方的办公室。

turns.speaker: Jacob Warwick
turns.en: It can be. But if I'm a product manager and I'm talking to a director, that may not be possible.
turns.zh: 可能确实如此。但如果我是产品经理和总监谈话，可能就做不到了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Right.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Jacob Warwick
turns.en: Right? You might just say, "Look, you got to come into the office. You got to do this." I'm pushing... When I'm talking about a C-suite level, you could pull them out of the office, "Hey, let's go get drinks." Sometimes, these deals are closed at 8:30 at night after a concert or something like that, so it's easing that situation. That being said, it doesn't mean you couldn't try. It's like, "Hey, I've got a couple questions. Are you open to take a walk down AT&T Park and have a conversation about it?" If you could pull them out of that, you can start to build a stronger relationship through that and you're more likely to get your way.
turns.zh: 是吧？你可能只会说：“听着，你得来办公室一趟。必须得做这件事。”我是在施压……当我说到高管层级时，你可以把他们从办公室拉出来，说：“嘿，咱们去喝一杯吧。”有时候，这些交易是在晚上8点半、一场音乐会结束后或者类似场合达成的，所以这能缓解紧张局面。不过，这并不意味着你就不能尝试。比如说：“嘿，我有几个问题。你介意去AT&T球场走一走，聊聊这事吗？”如果你能把他们从那种状态中拉出来，就能通过这种方式建立更牢固的关系，也更有可能达成你的诉求。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Talk us through the process you would recommend from, "I get an offer. Recruiter sends me. 'Here's your offer, 300K, salary, some kind of equity.'" What's the step by step you'd... And I know this depends on the role, seniority, type of company, PE, VC, back startup, because it's very scary to push back and be like, "Oh, I want more." What's that first email/reply to that email look like typically? What are some phrases maybe you'd use? And then how do you open up a conversation where you plan to ask for more if you're meeting in person, especially, because that feels so scary?
turns.zh: 请跟我们详细讲讲你建议的流程：比如，“我收到一个offer。招聘人员发邮件说：‘这是你的Offer，30万美元的年薪，还有一些股权。’”接下来该怎么做？我知道这取决于职位、资历、公司类型、私募股权、风险投资、初创公司等因素，因为直接反驳说“我想要更多”确实挺吓人的。通常第一封邮件/回复邮件应该怎么写？如果是面对面交流，又该如何开启讨价还价的对话呢？毕竟当面提要求确实更让人紧张。

turns.speaker: Jacob Warwick
turns.en: So, first, we want to approach with gratitude. We're thankful that we want to move forward, so, "Lenny, I appreciate you making me an offer. I'm excited to work with you." We want to show enthusiasm, which also shows some confidence. We have to show that the deal's going to get done even if you're on the fence about it. Now, it's not to say you're so excited that it's a sure thing and you're not showing that you're disappointed, even if you are, so, "I'm grateful. I'm looking forward to working with you. I want to review this over the next couple of days, talk to my wife about it, talk to an advisor, so and so." Later on, when you're a high level executive, you're talking to legal, you're talking to advisors, you're talking to a coach, you may have five or six people see that, employment lawyer, all that. That stuff is expected. (00:24:28): So you're going through the process, "I'm going to take a couple days to process this. I'll get back to you. I may have a couple of questions, but we'll loop back and it shouldn't be a problem. I imagine we start working together in a couple weeks." The point is you have to sell that the deal's going to be done, which helps them feel like it's going to move forward regardless. Any ask that you make is not going to be egregious. Now, oftentimes, the higher you anchor, the better you're going to perform, which can be frustrating because you don't necessarily want to be like, "Oh, I increased at 40%," or anything like that. (00:25:03): Now, this is where a lot of nuance comes in. We might say, "Come back three days later, want to have the conversation, let's take a walk in the park and talk through it. I got to be honest with you, where this offer stands right now, I don't feel comfortable moving forward. It's a little lighter than I expected." I may start saying something like that, and then just wait and see what they have to say. Maybe they say, "Well, what did you have in mind?" It's like, "Well, what's the chance you can share what the range looks like for this, and what type of performance did you expect for each of these levels?" Or they may say, "We comped you in the middle part of the range." You might say, "What does the top end look like? What must I do to fit those needs for you? Can you help me understand?" (00:25:47): Now, for a lot of folks, especially in this market, if we talk about what it was like in 2021 versus what it's like now, there's some overleveling that's happened. There are people that are C-suite going back to VP, and VP is going back to directors, especially as they go to bigger companies. Oftentimes, I'll say, "As we had this conversation, I'm likely a little more horsepower than you anticipated. What's the chance we can come in and restructure the comp for the type of talent we're bringing in here?" This is a line that we used. There was three folks last year that were in ranges of 185 to 285, that deal landed at 1.1 million when we were done with increases in stock, big cash increases, two deals that were comped at 600 that landed at 1.1 and 1.2, so doubled from that. And these were situations where the role started at senior director and were up-leveled to VP because they were reaching for top talent in that situation. So there are opportunities where it's easier to steer if you're really, really good. (00:26:53): I could see why some listeners are like, "Well, I'm not there in my career yet." In that case, this is just how it gets done. This is how bigger moves happen. It doesn't mean you can't push for maybe 20% more naturally. In that, I would start with, "What's the chance there's a little bit more here? I was expecting this." Again, more nuances because if you open up what you're looking for too early in the conversation, that can be difficult to come back from later on. It's not entirely egregious, but one of the first things out of a recruiter's mouth is, "How much money do you want to make?" which is eerily similar to an illegal question, which is, "How much money do you make?" But if you say, "What do you want to make?" then it's okay, and that's where a lot of people get hung up as well.
turns.zh:
首先，我们要以感恩之心开启谈话。我们要感激对方愿意向我们提供机会，说：“莱尼，感谢你给我这个提议。我很期待与你共事。”我们需要展现出热情，这也体现出自信。即便对方尚有犹豫，我们也要让他们相信交易能够达成。当然，这并不意味着你要表现得信心满满，也不要掩饰失望情绪。比如说：“我很感激，期待与你合作。接下来几天我会仔细评估，与妻子商量，再咨询顾问等。”  

当你成为高层管理者时，需要与法律团队、顾问、教练等多方沟通，这些步骤都是预料之中的。在此过程中，你要强调交易会顺利完成，让对方安心。“我需要几天时间考虑，之后再回复你。如果有疑问，我们可以再沟通，应该不成问题。我预计几周后就能正式合作。”关键在于要让对方相信交易会推进，而你的任何要求都不会过分。但有时，提价幅度过高反而适得其反，比如“我提价 40%”之类，这可能让对方反感。  

接下来是微妙的谈判阶段。比如：“三天后再谈，带你去散散步，聊聊细节。说实话，目前的报价让我不太安心推进。比预期低了不少。” 对方可能会问：“那你的期望薪资范围是多少？”你可以反问：“能透露一下他们的薪资区间吗？你对不同职级有怎样的业绩要求？” 对方可能会回应：“我们定在区间中段。” 你可以追问：“那上限是多少？我要达到哪些标准才能满足你的要求？” 

特别是在当前市场环境下，职级调整频繁。例如，C 级高管降级为副总裁，副总裁又降为总监，尤其是在大型企业中。你可以说：“根据我们的谈判，我可能比你们预期的更具价值。能否调整薪资结构以匹配我们引进的人才？” 去年有三个案例，原薪资区间 185-285，最终涨幅达 110%至 120%——从高级总监晋升为副总裁，吸引顶尖人才加入。这些情况下，如果你足够出色，谈判会更顺畅。  

有些听众可能会说：“我职业生涯还没到那一步。” 但这正是谈判的真谛。大动作往往源于此。当然，你也可以自然地争取 20% 的涨幅。首先要明确：“你期望的薪资区间是多少？”
会不会这里还有点额外信息？我原本还期待着别这样呢。”这里又有一些微妙之处，因为如果在谈话早期就暴露出你对薪资的期望，后续可能就很难再回头了。这倒不算太过分，但招聘人员最常开口问的第一个问题往往是“你希望赚多少钱？”，这和非法询问“你现在赚多少钱？”如出一辙。但如果你反问“你期望的薪资是多少？”，那就没问题了。但很多求职者也会在这点上卡壳。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that phrase you just shared of, "What's the chance there's a bit more here. I was expecting number X." Is that the phrase you recommend, that approach of just the soft pushback just to see?
turns.zh: 我很喜欢你刚刚分享的那句话：“这里多给一点的机会有多大啊？我原本期待的是X这个数字。”你推荐的这个方法，就是通过委婉地反驳对方，看看他们的反应吗？

turns.speaker: Jacob Warwick
turns.en: Sometimes. Again, it really depends on the leveling. If you are very senior, I typically don't want to re- anchor with a number because you should never be so sure of what you're worth that you wouldn't accept more. When you anchor, that's the ceiling, and what often happens is naturally they want to split the difference. (00:28:15): There's a quick Hollywood story here. We had a writer who had a $700,000 contract, so 700, and the agent that I was working with was saying, "This writer has the most aggressive attorneys in LA. They're super aggressive," and I said, "Well, how do you know, first of all, if that's what they're perceived as?" The production studio offers this writers 700. The attorneys come back and say, "We want 1.3, 1.3 million," and the studio said, "Fine, we'll do a million," and they settled at a million. And I find that really interesting because the studio came up 300,000, and the attorneys lost 300,000, so they split the difference right in the middle. So if the attorneys-
turns.zh: 有时候吧。这真的取决于谈判的水平。如果你职位很高，我通常不愿意用数字来设定底线，因为你永远不该对自己的价值如此确定，以至于不愿接受更高的报价。当你设定底线时，那就成了天花板，而通常对方会选择折中方案。（00:28:15）这里有个好莱坞的趣事。我们有个编剧签了70万美元的合同，数字是700，跟我合作的经纪人说：“这位编剧在洛杉矶有最强势的律师，他们特别好斗。”我说：“首先，你怎么知道他们被外界这么看待呢？”制片方给这位编剧开出70万美元报价，律师回来说：“我们要13万美元。”制片方说：“好吧，那就100万美元。”最后双方以100万美元达成协议。我觉得这很有意思，因为制片方提价了30万美元，而律师却让步了30万美元，双方最后在中间价上达成了妥协。所以如果律师——

turns.speaker: Jacob Warwick
turns.en: So you split the difference right in the middle. So if the attorneys said 1.5, would the deal have come in at 1.1? If the attorney said 1.7, would it have come in at 1.2? How do we know? (00:29:15): The way I see it is those attorneys weren't aggressive enough. We didn't find the ceiling there, did we? That was lazy negotiating. So it still made the client 300,000. They were excited. The attorneys were excited, they made more on their commission. The agency was excited, they got 10% of that. But we didn't find the ceiling, did we? That was lazy negotiating. (00:29:36): So those are things that you've got to slow down to really understand where is the value being made here? And that movie, that movie could make $50 million. You think one million for writing was worth it for someone who controlled the creative there? I don't know. A 50 to one value exchange, why not push for more? Why not put some milestones in that if this movie makes more than 50, my milestone is increased? This is how Tom Brady had his contract at Tampa Bay. Win eight games, get a half a million dollars. Win 12 games, get a million five. Go to the playoffs, get an extra this. Win the division, get this. Get to the Super Bowl, X. Win Super Bowl MVP, two and a half million more. So performance-based triggers.
turns.zh:
于是你就在中间找了个折中方案。那么，如果律师说1.5，那交易价会是1.1吗？如果律师说1.7，那会是1.2吗？我们怎么知道呢？（00:29:15）：在我看来，那些律师不够强势。我们没有找到交易的上限，对吧？这就是偷懒谈判的结果。所以客户还是赚了30万。他们很兴奋，律师也很兴奋，佣金赚得更多，经纪公司也分得了10%。但我们毕竟没找到上限，对吧？这就是偷懒谈判。
（00:29:36）：所以这些事情你得慢下来，才能真正理解价值在哪里创造？那部电影本可以赚5000万美元。你觉得对控制创意的人来说，100万美元的编剧费值得吗？我不知道。50比1的价值交换，为什么不争取更多？为什么不设定一些里程碑？如果电影票房超过5000万，我的里程碑就增加？这就是汤姆·布雷迪在坦帕湾的合同。赢8场比赛，奖金50万美元。赢12场比赛，奖金150万美元。进入季后赛，额外奖励。分区冠军，奖励更多。赢得超级碗MVP奖，奖励250万美元。所以是基于表现的激励机制。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love just how much you love this. It's just clear this is so interesting to you.
turns.zh: 我真心觉得你对这事儿特别着迷。很明显这对你来说太有趣了。

turns.speaker: Jacob Warwick
turns.en: It's really nerdy, I know. I've obsessed over it in a weird way, but I don't know. It's been kind of baked into my psyche for a long time, probably because I felt so powerless growing up that I'm so interested in how power works. And I was so scared to advocate for myself. And I was the least assertive person that you knew until I met my wife. And she taught me how to be assertive and now I'm off to the races, so that's been helpful.
turns.zh: 这确实有点书呆子气，我知道。我自己也莫名其妙地痴迷过，但我也不确定。可能这股执着早就刻在我的基因里了，大概是因为我成长过程中感到很无力，所以对权力运作特别感兴趣。以前我特别不敢为自己争取权益。遇到我妻子之前，我是最不自信的人。她教会了我如何坚定，现在我信心满满，这确实很有帮助。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: On that note, do these tactics work on kids and wives? Is this something that translates?
turns.zh: 说到这儿，这些策略对孩子和妻子管用吗？能照搬吗？

turns.speaker: Jacob Warwick
turns.en: Absolutely not. I would not recommend that, especially if your wife knows what you do for a living and hears you on the phone all the time. And you try to say, "What's the chance?" And she's like, "No chance. Don't pull that on me, I know what you're doing." (00:31:10): And toddlers are terrorists, so I haven't figured that one out. I've resort to bribes and maybe that is a little Machiavellian on the toddlers. You can be out of your mind working on that. But yeah, don't recommend it with your spouse.
turns.zh: 绝对不行。我不建议这么做，尤其是如果你妻子知道你做什么工作，还总听到你打电话谈判。然后你问：“成功几率有多大？”她会说：“一点机会都没有。别糊弄我，我知道你在干什么。”（00:31:10）：还有孩子简直就是小恐怖分子，到现在我还没搞懂怎么对付他们。我只能靠贿赂，但对付孩子这招可能有点玩阴的。你可能会为此抓狂。但千万别对配偶用这招。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I would pay a lot of money for a version of you for toddlers. Oh my God. It's like I try to negotiate with the other kid.
turns.zh: 我愿意花大价钱请个儿童版的你 Oh my God。就好像我试图和另一个孩子谈判一样。

turns.speaker: Jacob Warwick
turns.en: I think we all would-
turns.zh: 我觉得我们都会——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm like, "Three minutes." He's like, "Six." I'm like, "Four minutes." "No, six." He never budges [inaudible 00:31:39]-
turns.zh: 我说：“三分钟。”他说：“六分钟。”我说：“四分钟。”“不，六分钟。”他一动不让步 [00:31:39未录音] ——

turns.speaker: Jacob Warwick
turns.en: "Five minutes." He's like, "Eight."
turns.zh: “五分钟。”他说：“八分钟。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, exactly. Although sometimes [inaudible 00:31:43].
turns.zh: 是啊，就是这样。不过有时候 [00:31:43未录音] ——

turns.speaker: Jacob Warwick
turns.en: My son does that too. I go, "Do you want a binky?" And he goes, "Five binkies." And I go, "I don't know if we have five," and he's all, "10 binkies."
turns.zh: 我儿子也这样。我问：“你要奶嘴吗？”他说：“五个奶嘴。”我说：“我不知道我们有没有五个。”他又说：“十个奶嘴。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Whatever you need, I'll get it if you go to sleep.
turns.zh: 无论你需要什么，只要你睡着了，我都会去拿。

turns.speaker: Jacob Warwick
turns.en: Yeah. Yeah, please sleep.
turns.zh: 是啊。是的，请去睡吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: [inaudible 00:31:56]. Yeah. Yeah. We need this for toddlers. I would subscribe. Okay, so-
turns.zh: [00:31:56，语音不清]。是啊。是啊。我们需要这种产品给幼儿用。我会订阅的。好的，那么——

turns.speaker: Jacob Warwick
turns.en: Ms. Rachel's the closest thing we got.
turns.zh: 瑞秋女士是我们能找到的最合适的人选了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. Okay, so coming back to this compensation number, so you've touched on this a bit, and I think this is an important part of your advice is when the number question comes up, who should speak first? What should your approach be if they ask you this question of how much do you want to make?
turns.zh: 是啊。好的，回到这个薪酬问题，你之前已经稍微提到了这个，我认为这部分建议很重要。当被问到薪资问题时，谁应该先开口？如果他们问你希望赚多少钱，你该如何应对？

turns.speaker: Jacob Warwick
turns.en: Yeah, there's a decent amount of nuance in this too. So one thing you should realize is that especially earlier in your career, they're going to push on this harder. And that indicates that the person asking is really more looking for a commoditized or a price sensitive hire. That can be okay. There's nothing wrong with sharing your number and getting a deal that moves the needle early in your career and even middle of your career. That changes the higher up the ladder you go. And this is one of the reasons I want to share this is that what got you here won't get you there. So things start changing as you mature in your career. (00:32:57): So when you're working with a top recruiter, they don't ask you about comp. They won't. The problem is top recruiters only reach out to you when you're very well known and they don't reach out to you very often. It's very difficult to optimize for inbound attention the higher up you go unless you become very popular. And then what happens is you share less information because people come to you in a different capacity. (00:33:20): So nine times out of 10, a recruiter reaching out to you is going to ask that number. One time out of 10, they're going to just focus on the value creation. Those are the ones you want to focus on, the best possible. But it could be confusing because so often you get a different side of the story, more of the commodity type stuff. (00:33:40): So typically, I'd recommend you answer, right? "I don't talk about compensation until we're ready to make an offer, it sounds like we're pretty far away there. I'd love the opportunity to learn more about the team, understand where the value comes in, and proceed kind of down that path to make sure we're a good fit. Is that going to be a problem?" And then typically they'll say, "Yeah, it is going to be a problem. I just need to know a number." Right? (00:34:06): Now, it's very uncomfortable to do this back and forth and to say no, especially Americans have a hard time saying no. I have noticed that other cultures can be more direct and just say, "No, I'm not going to do it." So be it, right? So culturally, there's a lot of differences in how this conversation happens. (00:34:22): So they say, "Look, we need a number from you." You might say, "Look, I'm uncomfortable doing that right now because I don't understand the scope of the role. Can you help me understand what you had in mind?" (00:34:35): The reason I learned this is I used to be a marketing manager making $12 an hour in downtown San Francisco for Series A companies, not knowing that $12 an hour wasn't a lot of money, I just didn't know any better. But then I looked up marketing managers and I saw that they made 60 grand a year and I suddenly got offended in how little money I was making. Then I got promoted to director in that period and was making $14 an hour, good for me. And then I saw that marketing directors were making 110,000 at the time. (00:35:02): So when a recruiter called me, I pulled that. I didn't want to tell them I was making $14 an hour. They'd be like, "Who is this kid? He's not very good. That's fake title." And instead I said, "What did you have in mind?" And they said, "Oh, we're looking at 110 to 130." And I'd say, "Oh, I'm on the upper end of that now." So I went from $14 an hour to $120,000 a year in a single month, a single jump, just like that. That changed my life, one negotiation. It's one of the reasons I'm so passionate about that. (00:35:27): I hated the marketing work, for what it's worth, but I thought if I made a lot of money, it would make that pain go away of not liking my job. Turns out that was a fool's errand, but that's a story for another time.
turns.zh:
是的，这里面其实有很多微妙之处。你需要意识到，尤其是在职业生涯早期，他们会更强调这一点。这表明，面试官其实更倾向于寻找一个价格敏感型、可量化的候选人。这本身并无过错——在职业生涯早期或中期，通过分享薪资要求来快速达成协议也未尝不可。但随着职位晋升，情况会发生变化。这也是我想分享这些经验的原因：过去的成功经验未必能助你走得更远。

（00:32:57）：当你与顶级猎头合作时，他们不会主动询问薪资。但问题是，顶级猎头只有在你声名远扬时才会联系你，而且这种情况并不常见。除非你变得极具知名度，否则很难通过主动获取关注来提升自身价值。到那时，你分享的信息会变得有限，因为人们会以不同身份与你接触。

（00:33:20）：所以九成情况下，猎头联系你时都会询问薪资。但十次中有一次，他们只会关注价值创造。这才是你应该重点关注的——但这可能令人困惑，因为你常听到的是价格导向的信息。

（00:33:40）：通常我的建议是这样回答：“在我们准备提供Offer之前，我不会谈论薪资。看起来我们还早得很。我很希望能更多了解团队，理解价值创造的点，然后再判断是否合适。这会有问题吗？”对方通常会说：“没错，确实有问题。你必须给我个数字。”

（00:34:06）：这种反复周旋和拒绝对方要求的过程很令人不适，尤其是美国人很难说‘不’。我注意到其他文化更直接，会直接拒绝：“不行，我不接受。”那也无妨，文化差异很大。

（00:34:22）：对方会说：“你必须给我们个数字。”你可以说：“我现在没法给，因为我不了解职位的具体要求。你能帮我理解你们的期望吗？”  

（00:34:35）：我有过这样的经历——我在旧金山市中心的初创公司做市场经理，时薪12美元，完全不知道这很低。后来我查了市场经理的薪资标准，发现他们年薪6万美元。当时我涨到14美元，但仍远低于市场水平。

（00:35:02）：猎头联系我时，我隐瞒了真实薪资。他们会说：“这家伙谁啊？水平太差，职位虚高。”我反问：“你们的预期薪资是多少？”他们说：“11-13万。”我说：“我现在已经接近这个区间了。”就这样，我从14美元一小时，一跃升至12万美元年薪。一次谈判改变了我的命运。这也是我对此如此热衷的原因。

（00:35:27）：说实话，我讨厌市场营销工作，但只要能赚大钱，一切都值得。
希望讨厌这份工作带来的痛苦能随之消失。结果发现这根本就是徒劳一场，不过这事儿以后再细说吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Do things in your experience ever fall apart when you try to do that? Because that is a scary thing to push back on just like, "No, I'm not going to tell you number." And you're giving us advice on how to say it in a nice way and then just like, what did you have in mind? The fear is like, okay, they're going to hate me and they're going to be like, "Well, it's not worth it. We're going to move on." Has that ever happened? What are the odds that might happen?
turns.zh: 在你的人生经历中，当你试图做某件事时，是否曾遇到过事情一团糟的情况？因为要拒绝别人这样的要求实在太令人害怕了，比如“不，我不会告诉你那个数字的。”你给我们建议如何用委婉的方式拒绝，但随后你又会问：“你到底想说什么？” 那种恐惧感就像，"好吧，他们会讨厌我的，还会说，‘算了，不值得，我们还是放弃吧。’ 这种情况真的发生过吗？这种情况发生的概率有多大？

turns.speaker: Jacob Warwick
turns.en: A couple things about power. So if you have the ability to say no, you have infinite power. Right? The nuance changes when you don't have a job and you need to pay your mortgage, you might answer that differently because you want something. Right? (00:36:14): Now, this isn't to shame somebody who's feeling that way. If you're out of work for six weeks in San Francisco, you're homeless. That's just the reality of the situation. So if I got to say a number to get a job, I think that's fine. But understand that once you're employed and somebody's asking you and your needs are already getting met, why do you need to get pushed around? (00:36:34): This is one reason that it's easier to find a job when you have a job. Now, I think this is a myth, for what it's worth, but this is easier because naturally your needs are getting met financially to a degree. So naturally, you negotiate more confidently. When you're out of work and you have the uncomfort of being out of work six months, 12 months, 18 months, you have an identity tied to a chief product officer role or a VP of product. That's your identity in our country. We don't ask who you are and about your kids. We say, "What do you do for a living?" And when you are stripped of that title, it's uncomfortable and we want that pain to end. (00:37:10): So we give into these demands because it's an authoritative figure and we want that pain to go away. If we have the finances and the luxury of being able to say no, we increase our power. If we have the ability to push back and practice these difficult conversations, you will increase your power and you'll land at a higher rate because of it. (00:37:29): So can it get frustrated? Absolutely. But if somebody disrespects you through that process, doesn't that give you an indication of who the company's working with? Now again, I might accept that because I need the money, I understand. But it's very telling how somebody's going to treat you depending on very simple pushbacks. (00:37:48): And one behavioral psychology hack here is we give someone a positive reputation that they want to withhold, whether they deserve it or not. So in this instance, you'd say to the recruiter, "I want to thank you for being an advocate for me and for respecting that I won't share compensation figures right now. I appreciate that." And then they're trapped. They have to say, "No, I don't respect you. I have to do this." Or they have to say, "You're right, that makes sense. Let me move you forward or not." Right? (00:38:23): Another option, you don't necessarily know if you're the best solution for that fit or not. So we're obviously very ingrained, when a recruiter reaches out to you and they say, "Look, we're going to pay 120," and you make 150, and you're like, "Oh, I'm not interested. That's not even close." I would recommend continuing that process anyway to see as practice what you can negotiate and you can always say no later. Just because having that practice is going to make you hundreds of thousands, if not millions more in your career. (00:38:51): Alternatively, if you feel bad about, "Oh, I wasted their time because I was too much for what they needed," make recommendations for them. So when the offer comes in [inaudible 00:39:01] it was senior PM role and what you realized is the JD and all of the work that you did is actually a director role, but they're not going to pay for a director role. How often does that happen? You get to say, "Look, this role isn't in alignment with where we're headed. Would you like me to make an introduction to somebody that's a better fit?" So you still get to help them, you remove yourself. And then sometimes they say, "No, actually we do want the role to be more senior. We're going to extend for you." My first VP role came out of turning down a content manager position for 70,000. And six months later, I landed at VP for a quarter million. That was my first realm into VP. The initial offer was for content manager. So they came three, four levels up the food chain. That was a long negotiation, but these things can happen if you don't say no too quickly.
turns.zh:
关于权力的几个要点。比如，如果你有拒绝的能力，那你就拥有无穷的权力。对吧？但当你失业且需要还房贷时，情况就有所不同，你的回答可能会截然不同，因为你需要得到某些东西。是吧？（00:36:14）：现在，我不是要羞辱那些有这种感受的人。如果你在旧金山失业六周，你就无家可归。这就是现实。所以如果为了找到工作我必须妥协，我觉得这没问题。但要明白，一旦你就业了，别人问你需求是否被满足时，你为什么还要任人摆布？（00:36:34）：这就是为什么有工作时找工作更容易的原因。现在，我觉得这是一个误区，但确实更容易，因为你的财务需求在一定程度上得到了满足。所以你自然会更有底气地谈判。当你失业六个月、十二个月、十八个月时，人们只会关注你的职位头衔，比如首席产品官或产品副总裁。在我们国家，人们不会问你是谁，而是问你做什么工作。当你失去这些头衔时，那种不适感会让人想尽快摆脱这种困境。（00:37:10）：所以我们会屈服于这些要求，因为对方是权威人物，我们想摆脱这种痛苦。如果我们有财务能力和底气拒绝，就会增强自己的权力。如果我们有能力反击并进行这些艰难的对话，你的权力会提升，最终获得更高的报酬。（00:37:29）：这会让人感到沮丧吗？当然。但如果有人在过程中不尊重你，这不就说明公司在和什么样的人合作吗？现在，我可能会接受，因为我需要钱，我理解。但这种对待方式会暴露出对方的真实面目。（00:37:48）：这里有一个行为心理学技巧：我们会赋予别人一个他们想隐藏的积极形象，无论他们是否配得上。比如，你可以对招聘人员说：“感谢你为我争取权益，感谢你尊重我现在不想透露薪资的决定。”然后他们就被困住了。他们不得不说：“不，我不尊重你。我必须这么做。”或者他们不得不说：“你说得对，这很合理。让我推进你的申请吧。”对吧？（00:38:23）：另一种情况是，你不确定自己是否是最合适的人选。所以当招聘人员联系你说：“看，我们开120万，你现在挣150万，你说‘哦，我不感兴趣，差得太远了。’”我建议无论如何继续这个过程，看看你能争取到什么。以后你随时可以拒绝。毕竟，积累这些经验会为你的职业生涯带来数十万甚至数百万的价值。（00:38:51）：或者，如果你为自己的行为感到内疚，比如“哦，我浪费了他们的时间，因为我不符合他们的需求”，那就为他们提供建议。比如，当offer来的时候（00:39:01，原文缺失），职位是高级产品经理，但你发现JD和你的所有工作实际上对应的是总监级别，但他们不愿支付总监薪资。这种情况多吗？你可以说：“看，这个职位和我们的发展方向不符。你介意我帮你介绍其他人吗？”
“更适合他们？”所以你还是能帮到他们，但你得主动退出。然后有时他们会说：“不，实际上我们希望这个职位级别更高些。我们会为你延长合同。”我获得首个副总裁职位的机会，源于拒绝了一份年薪7万美元的内容经理职位。六个月后，我成功晋升为副总裁，年薪达25万美元。这是我踏入副总裁行列的第一步。最初的职位邀约是内容经理。但他们最终提出了比这高三、四级的职位。这次谈判历时很久，但只要你不轻易拒绝，这样的机会就可能降临。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Along these lines, I want to touch on, it feels like maybe the core approach you take, kind of the core to your philosophy, which is to kind of break out of this idea of some benchmark for a specific role and instead make it very clear to the company, "Here's the pain I will solve for you that is really important to you, and here's why it's worth paying me this much more because it's such a big problem for you." Talk about just that mindset.
turns.zh: 基于此，我想谈谈您的核心理念，您所秉持的核心哲学。您似乎在突破某个特定职位的固有标准，而是向公司清晰传达："我将为您解决至关重要的痛点问题，而这份高薪正是源于这个问题对您而言意义重大。"能否请您详细阐述这种思维模式？

turns.speaker: Jacob Warwick
turns.en: So this really comes down to having curiosity and showing curiosity about the actual problem because usually, if I'm speaking to a room of 400 people, which I'll occasionally do with some communities, I'll ask them who is actually doing the job that's on their job description? Nobody will raise their hand. It's not like you have your job description right there and that's what you do. There's always so much more that's not documented. Right? (00:40:44): Now, when you're going into a position and you see a JD, you're like, "Yeah, I could do all those things," but there's so much more. This is another reason that anchoring to a number too early is tough because you anchor to, "Oh, this is fair for a senior PM role." This is fair. Then you go through the process of the interviewing, it's very clear that it's a director role. You're going to lead five people. They scoop another team under you. "Oh, we're going to put a product-led growth motion under you too. There's a whole engineering pod and there's this and there's this. " All of a sudden, that's called scope creep. (00:41:17): So they scope creep the role, they talk about how they want a senior hire. They're excited about you, they get you excited about it. And then they give you the offer and it's actually 20% under the number you originally shared. And then you say, "Okay, well, this looks like a director role. I want X." And they say, "But you said you only wanted 140." Now they're using a number against you and it's very awkward to come back from that. So that's why we don't want to anchor too early, we want to understand. (00:41:43): So this is one thing I wish, especially product engineers, designers, that side of the product stack, I would love for you to treat more of these like a sales conversation. You are an enterprise solution, a consulting solution that is several hundred thousand dollars, if not millions of dollars a year. If you were to sell that product into an organization, think enterprise B2B deals, and I know I'm getting a little buzzwordy here, think an enterprise B2B deal to Salesforce and you're going to sell a million and a half dollar product. It would take you 18 months to develop the relationships and close that deal. (00:42:19): You have to develop champions in the organization. You have to understand what value you can create for each of those people so that they can advocate for you. You don't come in and pitch them the price right off the bat. You need to understand the value. (00:42:34): So through the process, it's a discovery process. Why am I here? What gets you excited about me? That's how we start a conversation. Too many interviews start with, "Tell me about yourself, tell me about this stuff in the past." If you're talking about your past, you're on the back foot and you're losing that conversation. You're the one revealing information, you're not getting anything. (00:42:56): We instead want to have a conversation and say, "Look, some of the best interviews I've always had felt a little bit more like consultations or brainstorming sessions. Are you open to having a chat like that today?" That's the first step. Typically, they say, "Yeah, that sounds way better than me trying to drill you with questions." (00:43:13): So let me ask you, what are some of the things that you're excited about? I imagine, Lenny, you're excited to talk to me because I can help some of your audience negotiate. You've seen proof where dozens of your subscribers have made more money with the article we wrote together. You've even seen that some of your guests, unknowingly, have been negotiated against with some of the work that I've done. Is there anything that I missed? What's exciting to you? (00:43:36): So I want to clarify why I'm in the room with you. So we do that as a PMO. Sounds like, now we move to labeling. It sounds like you have a challenge with this product line. It sounds like we need to move or ship product faster. It sounds like AI has been a problem and we need to shift towards native AI. Is there anything that I missed? Then they're revealing information, you take control of that conversation. And then we want to share, what have you done about it? How big of a problem is this in the organization? This is basically a SWOT analysis. What are some of the things you've done well? What are some of the areas that the team failed? What are some of the things we should be doing that we're not? And what are some of the things we absolutely shouldn't touch? (00:44:21): So I want to ask all these discovery questions. They're like, "Oh, look, it's a $10 million problem where we've gone through five different PMs in six months," and you're starting to understand where the dirty laundry in the company is. Then we get to sell the vacation. Then we get to say, "Look, all right, so fast-forward six months from now and we're working on this problem together and we've solved the churn in the engineering department," or in the design department or whatever. "We've solved that and we've got two product launches under our belt. When you head into that board meeting next, how can we ensure that your head is held high?" So what I'm doing is I'm psychologically walking them to a position of like a painless position. I've removed the friction and the pain from their shoulders and I forced them to visualize a utopian situation and who was right next to them doing that? I was. (00:45:17): So when it comes to your competition, there is no competition. I'm the only person who walked you into a vacation that you want to be in, looking forward to your head held high in a board meeting that's usually stressful, but instead this time, because you worked with me, it's not stressful. Then all of a sudden when it comes to the offer stage, there may be five other PMs, but I can only imagine working with Jacob. So when I push back, the likelihood that I break the rules is significantly higher than if I hadn't done that.
turns.zh:
因此，这实际上归结于保持好奇心，并对实际问题表现出兴趣。因为通常，如果我面对一个400人的听众（我偶尔会与一些社区进行这种交流），我会问他们，谁真正在做职位描述中的工作？没人会举手。并不是说你手头就有职位描述，然后你就必须严格按照那份描述行事。总有很多未被记录下来的额外工作，对吧？（00:40:44）：现在，当你应聘一个职位时，看到职位描述时，你会想，"是的，我能胜任所有这些任务。"但实际上远不止如此。这也是为什么过早锁定薪资标准很困难的原因——你可能认为"高级产品经理的职位薪资是合理的"，但实际面试过程中发现这只是总监级别。你需要领导五个团队，还要负责产品主导的增长策略，还有整个工程团队……突然之间，这就成了范围蔓延的问题。（00:41:17）：他们不断调整职位要求，声称需要高级人才。他们对你热情高涨，让你也为之兴奋。然后给你offer，薪资却比你最初提出的低20%。你会说，"好吧，看起来这是总监级别，我想要X。"他们却说，"但你之前只说要140。"现在他们用数字反过来压你，想要翻盘局面太难了。所以我们不希望过早锁定标准，而是要先了解情况。（00:41:43）：所以我希望，尤其是产品工程师和设计师——产品栈的这部分群体——能更把这当作销售对话来对待。你就是一款企业级解决方案，一套咨询方案，每年价值几十万甚至上百万美元。假如你要把这款产品卖给一家企业，考虑B2B交易（我知道我用了点行话），就拿Salesforce的案例来说，你要卖一款150万美元的产品。开发客户关系并完成交易需要18个月。（00:42:19）：你必须在组织中培养拥护者。要明白你能为每个关键人物创造什么价值，这样他们才能为你发声。你不能一开始就直接报价。要先理解价值。（00:42:34）：所以整个过程就是一个探索过程。为什么我来这里？什么让你对我感兴趣？这才是对话的起点。太多面试都是从"介绍一下你自己，讲讲你过去的经历"开始的。如果你一直在谈论过去的经历，就处于被动地位，无法掌握对话主动权。你在主动透露信息，而对方却没有获取任何信息。（00:42:56）：相反，我们希望能开展对话，比如说："看，我参加过的最好的面试更像是一次咨询或头脑风暴会议。你今天愿意参与这样的对话吗？"这才是第一步。通常对方会说，"是啊，这比我用问题反复盘问你好多了。"（00:43:13）：那我问你，你对哪些方面感兴趣？我猜，Lenny，你很兴奋能和我交流，因为我能帮助你的一些读者进行谈判。你已经看到证据，数十位订阅者通过我们共同撰写的文章赚到了更多钱。你甚至注意到一些嘉宾
无意间，我的工作成果竟成了别人谈判的筹码。我是否遗漏了什么？有什么令你兴奋的事？  
（00:43:36）：所以我想先澄清一下，我为什么会和你们坐在一起。作为项目管理办公室（PMO），我们会做这些工作。听起来，现在你们要转向标签化了。看起来你们在这一产品线上面临挑战。听起来我们需要加快产品交付或发货速度。听起来AI一直是个问题，所以我们需要转向原生AI。还有什么我没提到的地方吗？  
 然后他们开始透露信息，这时你要掌控对话。接着我们想了解，你们为此采取了哪些措施？这个问题在组织中有多严重？这基本上就是SWOT分析。你们做得好的地方有哪些？团队失败的领域有哪些？我们应该做但没做的事有哪些？还有哪些事绝对不能碰？  
（00:44:21）：所以我想问所有这些探索性问题。他们可能会说：“哦，看吧，这是一个1000万美元的问题，过去六个月我们换了五个产品经理。”这时你开始了解公司内部的深层问题。然后我们就可以推销我们的假期方案了。接着我们会说：“好的，六个月后我们一起解决了工程部门的流失问题”，或者设计部门的问题。这些问题解决后，我们还成功推出了两款产品。下次你参加董事会会议时，我们如何确保你能昂首挺胸？”  
所以我的做法是从心理上引导他们进入一个轻松的状态。我为他们消除了阻碍和压力，迫使他们构想一个理想的场景，而站在他们身边实现这一切的人是谁？是我。  
（00:45:17）：说到竞争对手，这里其实没有竞争对手。我是唯一一个带你进入理想状态的人，让你期待在通常充满压力的董事会会议上昂首挺胸。而这次，因为你与我合作，压力不再。然后到了报价阶段，可能有五个其他产品经理，但我相信合作体验只有与雅各布在一起才会如此美好。所以当我据理力争时，突破规则的可能性要比不这样做大得多。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is amazing. So trying to just summarize what you're sharing here, and I think it's important for people to also note, you can do it in your own words. This is likely not something you'll just be able to pop out and do. This is something that takes time to do well and it feels awkward probably. And that's why people work with you that you probably role play and all these things, but still, there's things people can pull out of this that they can do on their own.
turns.zh: 这太令人惊叹了。所以，我想简要总结一下你在这里分享的内容，我认为这对大家来说很重要，你们也可以注意到，你可以用自己的话来表达。这可能不是你能随口就做出来的事情。这需要花时间才能做好，可能还会让人感到不自在。这就是为什么人们会与你合作——你可能进行角色扮演之类的活动，但即便如此，人们仍能从中汲取一些可自行运用的经验。

turns.speaker: Jacob Warwick
turns.en: It could be tricky to understand where your value is because you're so close to it. You just do this every day. And for product folks that only listen to product folks and are in the product ecosystem in your bubble, Lenny, they're not seeing the impact on marketing. They're not having those conversations necessarily. So it's so ingrained in everything that you do that you could functionally be excellent, but in order to break these boundaries, you have to be cross-functionally understanding how it impacts others and the motivations of others. That's when things really start to unlock. And that's where just understanding a little perspective can be helpful in that outside influence there.
turns.zh: 要理解自己的价值所在可能很困难，因为你离它太近了。你每天都在做这些事。而对于那些只听产品从业者讲话、深陷产品生态圈的“泡泡”里的产品从业者来说，他们看不到对市场营销的影响。他们也不一定会参与这类讨论。因此，你所做的一切都与产品密不可分，你或许能把事情做得很好，但要突破这些界限，你必须跨职能地理解它对他人的影响以及他人的动机。只有这样，事情才会真正迎刃而解。这时，稍微了解一下外界的观点或许会有所助益。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think this is important to just briefly summarize your approach. So the idea here is figure out in many ways what matters most to them, what problems do they have, what they see in you, just like understand the landscape of where you could bring tons of value. Help them see that, like, "Here's the problem that I can help you with. Here's the problem that you have that we need ... Here's the many problems that we can help you with." And then help them visualize, you described it as sell to vacation, help them visualize, okay, now that this is solved, how awesome would that be? And part, there's like all this psychological stuff you're throwing in there, just like how [inaudible 00:47:25].
turns.zh: 我认为简要总结你的方法很重要。所以这里的核心思路是，想尽各种办法弄清楚对他们最重要的是什么，他们面临着哪些问题，或者他们在你身上看到了什么——总之，要了解你能创造巨大价值的领域。帮助他们认识到，“这里有我能帮你解决的问题。这里有你面临的、我们需要解决的问题……这里还有许多我们能帮你解决的问题。” 然后帮助他们想象，你把它描述成“推销度假产品”，帮助他们想象，好，问题解决了，那该有多棒？这里还涉及到一些心理层面的东西，比如[00:47:25处听不清]。

turns.speaker: Jacob Warwick
turns.en: Yeah. I can really make this concrete with a quick story.
turns.zh: 是的。我可以用一个简短的故事来具体说明。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. Let's do it.
turns.zh: 是的。我们来试试吧。

turns.speaker: Jacob Warwick
turns.en: So there's a very famous musician who was born the same year as me, for those super sleuths out there, who had a tour, a billion dollar tour and a documentary. And the director of said tour was a hot commodity in Hollywood. Every agency wanted to sign this director. This director didn't want to just do movie documentaries, right? Wanted to start producing actual movies. That's the dream. Right? (00:47:57): So every agency wanted to sign this hot director who just did this billion dollar deal with, people already know who it is. So my client, the agent asked me like, "We got to sign this. It would be stupid to go to any other agency. We've done this, we've done that, we've represented Julia Roberts and Matt Damon," and all this, just naming, name dropping, right? Now, this is actually a problem because if we're leaning on logic and credibility, we're losing. We need to sell the future and own the emotion. (00:48:29): So she just asked me, "How do we close this deal?" And to me, this was very simple. I said, "If you already had the job, who would you introduce him to? If you already had it, the deal's already signed, so put yourself in the position that you're already doing the job." That's why an interview process, if you treat it like you're consulting, you're doing a value exchange and you're increasing your value and you're asking the right questions. If you feel like you're on the outside and you're having to say, "Well, look, Lenny, I did this and I did that, and did you see I have three million words written? Why wouldn't you want to be the guest?" I don't care about what you've done, I care about what you'll provide my audience. Right? (00:49:08): So in this deal, we get into the meeting, it's a big day. And I said, "Schedule the appointment already, work with the assistant, schedule the appointment with whoever it is it needs to be. It needs to be a big name person." So we go into that interview and inevitably the conversation goes, "Why should I sign your agency?" So my client says, "What are you doing on Friday? I cleared a lunch with your assistant." And he says, "Well, I guess I'm going to lunch." And she's like, "Great, I'll have you meet Steven." And he said, "Steven who?" And she said, "Steven Spielberg." (00:49:43): And then some form after that, it was, "Where do I sign?" Because the meeting was already set with Steven Spielberg. For somebody who wants to get into film production, what better meeting to have. So for the other agencies, they're like, "We're the greatest thing. We've represented this director that did this media tour and we did that." They lost because we sold a vacation and we made it a reality right then and there and the value was clear.
turns.zh: 有一位和我同年出生的知名音乐家，对那些超级侦探们来说可能并不陌生。他举办了一场价值数十亿美元的巡演，还拍了一部纪录片。这场巡演的导演在好莱坞可是炙手可热的人物，每家经纪公司都想签下他。但这位导演不满足于只拍纪录片，而是想转型制作正片。这才是梦想，对吧？（00:47:57）：所以每家经纪公司都想签下这位刚完成数十亿美元交易的炙手可热导演，相信大家都知道是谁。我的客户，也就是那位经纪人，对我说：“我们必须签下他。去其他公司简直是疯了。我们有过辉煌业绩，代理过朱莉娅·罗伯茨和马特·达蒙等大牌明星。”然后就开始列举一长串客户名单，炫耀自己的人脉资源。（00:48:29）：但这其实是个误区——如果我们只依赖逻辑和声誉，就会输掉这场博弈。我们需要传递未来愿景，激发客户的情感共鸣。（00:49:08）：所以她问我：“怎么才能敲定这笔交易？”我回答：“如果你已经拿下这个职位，你会向谁推荐他？如果合同已经签了，就把自己代入那个角色。”这就是为什么在面试过程中，如果你以顾问的姿态参与，进行价值交换、提升自身价值并提出正确的问题，就能取得成功。如果你表现得像个局外人，拼命强调“看，我做过这个，那个，还有三百万字的作品集！你为什么不选我做嘉宾？”那我就只关心你能为我的客户创造什么价值，而不是你的过往成就。（00:49:43）：在这次会面前，我们做了充分准备。会议当天，我说：“赶紧安排见面，和助理协调时间。一定要找个大牌。” 会面中，对方不可避免地问：“为什么要签你们公司？”客户回应：“周五你有空吗？我和你的助理约了午餐。” 对方说：“那好吧，我去吃午餐。”客户又说：“太好了，我带你去见史蒂文·斯皮尔伯格。” 对方问：“史蒂文·斯皮尔伯格？” 客户答：“史蒂文·斯皮尔伯格。” 接下来，自然而然地就签约了。因为史蒂文·斯皮尔伯格的会面早已安排妥当。对于想进军电影制作领域的人来说，还有比这更棒的会面机会吗？其他经纪公司只能说：“我们才是最棒的。我们代理过那位巡演导演，干过这个干过那个。” 但他们输了，因为我们卖的是一个梦想的假期，并当场将其变为现实，价值一目了然。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So there's both this mindset shift of I'm going to try to actually help you figure out where I can be helpful and where the problems are and then start actually thinking about how to fix this. And also there's like, try to even do it. It sounds like you could just do it.
turns.zh: 所以这既需要转变思维模式——我要努力帮客户找到自己的价值所在，识别问题根源，然后开始思考如何解决问题——也需要付诸行动。听起来做起来挺简单的。

turns.speaker: Jacob Warwick
turns.en: If you can do it. So one of the tricks of my business is I can plant seeds with my clients really easily because I'm on the phone with somebody and I'm understanding who they need to connect with. So they might say, "Oh, I've been interested in getting to Google," or whatever. Let's say they're in product. I said, "Oh, I have somebody in product at Google. Let me make a text for you real quick." And I'll just do it while I'm on the phone with them. "Just hold on a second, hold on." (00:50:49): And then what happens is they get the beep. That's reciprocity. I'm triggering a reciprocity imbalance. And then I'm making another one for them. So I'll sometimes do two or three introductions right then and there and they see the value before I'm even off the phone. What I've also done is I've given three different touchpoints where I can make sure that that person is following through. I can get a 360 degree view of that person. I can ask one of those people to prompt them to close with me if I need to sell a deal. I'm getting a reciprocity imbalance. So what I want to do is show that I have the resources to support them, whether they sign a contract or not, and that's where we go. (00:51:27): And in this instance, if you want to role play with me for a second, something that would be really exciting, like Lenny, I want to understand what's exciting to you. If today's podcast was the best podcast, the highest performing podcast that had ever happened, what would that mean to you? And also, what did we do to make it so successful? What are the comments that people had to put down below? What are the things they said to make you feel like my conversation with Jacob was the best conversation I had all year? What would that look like to you?
turns.zh: 假如你能做到的话。我的业务秘诀之一就是能很轻松地为客户播下合作的种子——比如我在和某人通电话时，就能准确理解他们需要与谁建立联系。他们可能会说：“哦，我一直想进军谷歌领域。”或者假设他们从事产品开发工作。我会说：“哦，我在谷歌有位产品开发方面的熟人。我马上帮你发条消息过去。”然后就直接在通话中操作。“稍等片刻，稍等一下。”（00:50:49）接下来，对方会收到提示音。这就是互惠原理。我先制造一个互惠失衡，再为他们创造另一个互惠机会。有时我会当场为他们牵线两三个人，这样他们在挂断电话前就能感受到价值。我还会设置三个触点来确保对方能跟进。我可以全方位了解对方的情况。必要时，我会让其中一人协助我促成交易。这样就能制造互惠失衡。我的目标是向对方表明，无论是否签约，我都能为他们提供支持，这就是关键所在。（00:51:27）举个例子，如果你想和我角色扮演一下会很有趣。比如，莱尼，我想了解什么能让你兴奋不已。如果今天的播客是史上表现最佳、最成功的播客，对你意味着什么？我们又做了哪些让它如此成功的努力？听众在评论区写了什么？是什么让他们觉得我和雅各布的对话是我今年最棒的谈话？这对你来说意味着什么？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I immediately love this question as a ... It sounds to people like this is manipulative in ... It could come across as that as an external observer, but to me, I'm like, "This is exactly what I want to achieve." And I love that you're thinking about this and I want you to be focused on this and I would do a lot to help make this happen. (00:52:17): I guess to answer your question, I would just love it to be very concrete tactical advice that people can use to help negotiate their comp. And they spread this with all their friends, they're like, "This is the best thing I've ever heard around comp."
turns.zh: 我立刻就喜欢上了这个问题……在外人听来，这可能显得很操控……但对我来说，我觉得“这正是我想要达成的目标”。我很高兴你能思考这个问题，我希望你能专注于此，我愿意竭尽全力帮助实现这一目标。（00:52:17）我想回答你的问题，我希望能提供非常具体的实战建议，让人们能用这些方法来协商佣金。然后他们会把这些分享给所有朋友，说：“这是我听过关于佣金最棒的建议。”

turns.speaker: Jacob Warwick
turns.en: And one of the things that we can do is that we plant what you want someone to say in that conversation as well. So when I'm talking to these executives and I'm making the introductions, sometimes I'll ask, or an introductions come to me, I'll be curious like, "When you go back and you share with a friend, what are you going to say about me? Are you going to say Jacob was really helpful or are you going to say that Jacob's an asshole? I'm curious." (00:52:51): And sometimes I just make a complete reframe so there's no other option. Well, I'm obviously not going to say you're an asshole, so I'm going to say you're the great thing that I want you to say. I'm controlling the narrative I want them to perpetuate. So in this instance, and maybe some of your readers are going to be like, "This guy's a total manipulative jerk." I will say, I hope that you use this for good and not evil, but this is just the way power works. (00:53:14): I would hope that in the comment section, you say, "Lenny, this was such a refreshing and energetic podcast. This is what we want more of. This is exciting. We've done a lot of stuff in AI. This was very cool and different." Right? So I'm suggesting if you felt that way, share something like that below. Too many YouTube videos are like, "Oh, like and subscribe." And that's all they do, which does trigger action. It's a very simple thing. But when it comes to navigating your net worth and negotiating for power, these executives at the top control what every other person is saying, naturally. They know when somebody's talking about them when they're not in the room and they not only know about it, but they know what they said about them. (00:53:59): Similar to when somebody's like, "Oh, Lenny, we're going to do reference checks on you." What's the first thing you do? You call all those references and you say, "What are you going to say about me?" Ideally, you can control that to some capacity and improve the likelihood of you moving forward. So we already do this. We just have to integrate it into some everyday conversations and you can better control outcomes. (00:54:21): It's the same, interview process. When you go back to your committee, are you going to say, "Jacob solved X, Y, Z and we're excited. Slam dunk, let's move forward." And I like really quickly, slam dunk. Right? Easy to remember. Or are you going to say, "There's a couple gaps here in some of the competitors that we have or some of the competition seems more fulfilling." And I want to ask for that feedback while I'm still on the call with you. And I want to wait for an email to say, "I'm sorry you're not a fit." And then you ask for feedback and you don't get any. I have to do it while we're live in person because you can't deny me in that moment without it being awkward. (00:54:57): So what are you going to say? Is this a slam dunk? What's one thing I should have asked that I didn't? What are some areas that the other candidates excelled that you wish I showed more of? I want to understand where those gaps are so I have an opportunity to address them. And then if I didn't make the mark, I'd say, "I'd love to have a conversation with you next Thursday to talk through that in more detail. Thank you for bringing that to my attention." If you close the next conversation, you don't give up necessarily. That was another monologue, but that was a little bit inside the mind of how I think about these things.
turns.zh: 其中一件事是，我们可以提前构思好希望对方在谈话中说出的话。比如，当我与这些高管交谈并进行介绍时，有时我会问，或者对方会主动提问，我会好奇地问：“当你回头和朋友分享时，你会怎么说我？你会说雅各布很帮忙，还是说雅各布是个混蛋？我很好奇。”（00:52:51）有时我会完全重构局面，让对方别无选择。显然我不会说你是个混蛋，所以我会说你是我希望他们传播的正面形象。我在控制我想让他们延续的叙事。在这种情况下，也许有些读者会说：“这家伙完全是个操纵欲强的混蛋。” 我要说，我希望你们能善加利用，但权力就是这样运作的。（00:53:14）我希望在评论区，你们会说：“莱尼，这期播客太令人耳目一新、充满活力了。这正是我们所期待的。太令人兴奋了。我们在人工智能领域做了很多工作。太酷了，太与众不同了。” 对吧？所以如果你们有这种感觉，请在下方分享类似内容。太多YouTube视频只是说：“哦，点赞并订阅。” 这就是他们所做的，确实能引发行动。这很简单。但当涉及到管理个人声誉和争取权力时，这些高层自然会控制别人对他们的评价。他们知道别人在不在场的情况下谈论他们，不但知情，还清楚别人怎么说他们。（00:53:59）类似地，当有人说：“哦，莱尼，我们要对你的背景做参考调查。” 你第一时间会怎么做？你会打电话给所有推荐人问：“你们会怎么评价我？” 理想情况下，你可以一定程度上控制局面，增加成功的机会。所以我们已经在这么做了。我们只需将其融入日常对话中，就能更好地控制结果。（00:54:21）面试过程也是如此。当你回到委员会时，你会说：“雅各布解决了X、Y、Z问题，我们很兴奋。完美达成，继续推进吧。” 我喜欢简洁明了的说法。容易记住。对吧？还是你会说：“我们的一些竞争对手有一些空白，或者他们的方案看起来更具吸引力。” 我希望在通话时就提出这些反馈，而不是等邮件回复后才得知“很遗憾你不合适”。然后你提出反馈却得不到回应。我必须在当面交流时提出，因为当面拒绝会比较尴尬。（00:54:57）那么你会怎么说？这是否完美达成？我有没有遗漏的该问的问题？其他候选人哪些方面表现出色，而你希望我能更多展示这些？我想了解差距所在，这样我就有机会改进。如果我没能留下好印象，我会说：“下周四我很乐意与你进一步探讨。感谢你提出这些问题。” 即使对话结束，也不意味着放弃。这又是一段独白，但它能让你深入了解我思考这些问题的思路。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: No, this is so awesome. So if you think about a hiring manager, having someone like, I don't know, just imagine I'm interviewing for a role. If I come to them and say, "Here's the problem. I'm going to solve churn for you. I'm going to fix your onboarding flow. I'm going to figure out how to level up your design experience because I know that these are big challenges for you right now." If I was the hiring manager, I'd be like, "Holy shit, this is awesome. I just need someone to come in and solve these problems for me. This is why I'm hiring."
turns.zh: 太棒了！所以如果你站在招聘经理的角度想想，比如，我不知道，就假设我在面试一个职位。如果我去对他们说：“问题是这样的，我要帮你们解决客户流失问题。我要优化入职流程。我要提升你们的设计体验，因为我知道这些都是你们目前面临的重大挑战。”如果我是招聘经理，我肯定会说：“天哪，太棒了！我正需要有人来帮我解决这些问题。这就是我招聘你的原因。”

turns.speaker: Jacob Warwick
turns.en: And you better deliver. Right?
turns.zh: 而你最好能兑现承诺，对吧？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And you-
turns.zh: 而你——

turns.speaker: Jacob Warwick
turns.en: And that's the other thing. It sounds like if this guy can't deliver, it's not going to happen. Or if this gal can't deliver, that's frustrating. I'm not suggesting go so far outside of your comfort zone that you feel like you can't deliver because that reputation will haunt you. You have to really understand. (00:56:21): And I would also add that I wouldn't be so sure that I'm going to fix the onboarding flow. I wouldn't be so sure of that. I'm not so sure that you know that's the problem yet. The longer we can drag out the hiring process, and this sounds like pulling teeth, especially when you're unemployed. I just want the pain to be over. I'm asking you to slow it down. The more you slow down the process, the more you fight back about the manufactured urgency of us needing to get into that role sooner, the more information you're going to understand about that company and how you could really help. (00:56:54): So you could say, "Lenny, I hear that you want to fix the onboarding flow. I hear that. I hear this, but it sounds like that product might be deprecated anyway in this wave of AI. Is that a possibility?" What I don't want to do is prioritize something that the team's going to cut, right? That's going to hurt the P&L or whatever. Now, I can only ask that question if I've truly asked the right questions to understand. (00:57:18): So you may come in, this is the same concept as never be so sure of your worth that you wouldn't accept more, you're so sure of the job description, that they need these three things, that you don't even try to ask the questions to understand what the deeper problem is. And this going back also to why founders might be frustrated with my talk track, I'm not asking for you to take your pie and give them a bigger slice. I'm asking for you to work with somebody to expand the pie so everybody gets bigger slices. That's the plan. (00:57:48): And if you train your candidates and you're more revealing, and if their performance is tied to it, naturally they need to ask more questions to understand how to make it true. That's what we want, that's putting companies up and to the right.
turns.zh: 关键是，如果这个人兑现不了承诺，那就没戏了。或者如果这个人做不到，那就很让人失望。我不是建议你挑战自己的舒适区，让自己觉得无法胜任，因为这种名声会跟随你很久。你必须要真正理解。（00:56:21）：而且我还要补充一点，我不确定你能否优化入职流程。我不确定你是否真的了解这是个问题。我们越是拖延招聘过程，这听起来就像拔牙一样痛苦，尤其是当你失业的时候。我只想快点结束痛苦。我建议你放慢节奏。你越是拖延这个过程，越是反击那种“我们必须尽快填补这个职位”的虚假紧迫感，你就能收集到越多关于公司的信息，也能更好地理解自己如何能真正提供帮助。（00:56:54）：所以你可以说：“莱尼，我听说你想优化入职流程。我听说了。我听说了这些，但听起来这个产品可能在AI浪潮中被淘汰了。这有可能吗？”我不想做的是把优先级排得太高，以至于团队会裁掉它，对吧？那会损害利润表之类的。现在，我只有在真正问了正确的问题、理解了情况后才能提出这个问题。（00:57:18）：所以你可能会进来，这里和之前的理念一样，不要对自己的价值太过自信以至于不愿意接受更多薪酬，要对职位描述太过确定，以至于不去探究更深层的问题。这又回到了为什么创始人可能会对我的讲话内容感到不满的地方。我不是要你拿走你的那份馅饼，给他们更大的一块。我是让你和别人合作，把馅饼做大，让每个人都能分到更大的一块。这就是计划。（00:57:48）：如果你培训你的候选人，你更开放，如果他们的表现与此挂钩，他们自然会提出更多问题，去理解如何实现这一目标。这就是我们想要的，这就是让公司向上向右发展。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I like that you went there around don't-
turns.zh: 我喜欢你提到不要——

turns.speaker: Jacob Warwick
turns.en: ... putting companies up into the right.
turns.zh: ……让公司向上向右发展。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I like that you went there around, "Don't overpromise because it's easy to say. We're going to solve all your pain for you. I'm going to be the best thing to ever happen."
turns.zh: 我喜欢你提到：“不要做出过高的承诺，因为说起来容易。我们要为你解决所有痛点。我会成为你遇到的最棒的人。”

turns.speaker: Jacob Warwick
turns.en: You never under promise, over deliver. Always. Under promise, over deliver.
turns.zh: 你永远不要低估承诺，超额兑现。永远如此。低估承诺，超额兑现。
